Environment Variables and process.env

Config that lives outside the code, and how Node reads it.

Laravel keeps per-environment config (DB credentials, app URL, debug flags) in a .env file, read via env('KEY') or config(). The underlying mechanism — environment variables, a plain key/value store the operating system hands to whatever process it starts — isn't a Laravel invention; Node reads the exact same kind of values, just via a different object: process.env.

Figure 1.12 is this project's entry point:

// Figure 1.12: starting the server (src/server.js)
import app from './app.js';
import env from './config/env.js';

app.listen(env.PORT, () => {
  console.log(`Support Desk API listening on http://localhost:${env.PORT}`);
});

app.listen(port, callback) is what actually opens a port and starts accepting connections — the one thing app.js deliberately never does itself (see the comment at the top of that file, first topic). The port number comes from env.PORT, not a hardcoded 3000 — so the same code can run on whatever port a given machine (a teammate's laptop, a Docker container, a hosting platform) needs it to, without editing source code.

env here isn't process.env directly — it's this project's own src/config/env.js, which reads process.env and validates it. That's the next slide.
